questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Good weather, cheap living, totally different culture

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
First, I'm really glad I did it!
The less good things were the low quality of the studies, low efficiency of the university system, and that most students were there for being social 24/7 and going out partying as much as possible - which is not for me

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite challenging. Their website is not very logical. However, they are good at answering per mail and they mostly want to be helpful

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: None. I was assigned a voluntary buddy through ESN but never used it.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: In the beginning I sometimes felt like an administration worker because I had to spent so much time in front of my computer, finding out how to do everything

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Quite easy

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: In the accommodation-Facebook group make a post about yourself and what kind of accommodations and roommates you're searching. That helped me a lot and I was offered several accommodation opportunities. To avoid scammers, it's good to make a deal with the landlord that you won't pay before you see the apartment and get the keys.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There're so many opportunities and for a good price. However, many apartments are quite shitty so it's worth to search for apartments some good time in advance. Though, I found mine just 3 weeks before arrival.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Registration for all courses took 6 weeks!

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I had to get an Erasmus card in one building and register in another building in the other end of the city where I was met by a very unhelpful guy at the office who told me that I had to have a Greek phone number to register even though I brought all the documents needed in print and he could've used my Danish phone number or email for contact. Also, as several courses were cancelled and I had to attend courses of 30 ECTS it was hard to find new courses with the right amount of ECTS points and it was complicated finding out which courses from other schools that I could take as the professors all were confused about the rules

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The professors were generally really kind and tried to help even though they often didn't help much. The system quite inefficient and it seems like everyone was confused

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I had to change 2-3 courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: As they most often insist that you have a Greek number, just get it, and change back to your danish number after you receive the registration code. To receive the full Erasmus grant remember to registrade as soon as possible and check out as late as possible. Many students forgot about this and lost a part of the grant though they were obliged to receive the full.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Generally, very low quality. But the good thing is that when you're not busy with the studies you have a lot of time to travel, go out, meet people, and enjoy Greece

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Low. 
I learned a lot in one course, Modern Balkan History, but it was mostly because of home studying. It was really interesting and it has made me so much more interested in the Balkan countries and the history which also developed when I travelled in Albania, Montenegro and Kosovo after my final exam in Thessaloniki

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Much lower quality. Not academic level. Felt more like a friendly conversation or a chill workshop.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Language of Propaganda in the Media, Modern Balkan History, Travel Journalism, Intercultural Communication, Writing for the Broadcast Media,

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Modern Balkan History - but you have to actually make an effort and read for it to be interesting.

Intercultural Communication - the highest level of teaching and content.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The rent was 1650 kr. per month excluding gas and electricity. The gas and electricity bills varied a lot and were sometimes high and therefore unexpected.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were the same price as in Denmark and often even higher. However, buying fruit and vegetables at the food markets were much cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Many opportunities for amazingly beautiful trips for low costs! Also, the tavernas everywhere mostly offered great food for reasonable prices.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Fitness, trips to towns and nature, dinners, and a lot of parties hosted by the voluntary group ESN!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: As I'm just to train a lot of crossfit in Denmark, I found a great crossfit center just outside Thessaloniki where II attended classes 3 times a week and really enjoyed it. Here, there were only locals (and a couple of friends I brought from the university), and it was cool to interact with other people than just Erasmus students, and of course because they were locals and so kind and funny!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Nature in Greece: especially the Islands Thassos and Skopelos, the mountains in Northern Greece, and the beaches of Halkidiki.
The bordering countries - I really enjoyed going to North Macedonia, Bulgaria, Kosovo, Albania, and Montenegro. Many students also went to Istanbul and had a great time.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
The first month I was really frustrated about the inefficient university system. But when the registration were done, it was actually not hard adapting to the culture. It was nice that there were never any stress and the Greek people are amazing. So kind and helpful. The service at the tavernas are some of the best I've experienced in any country. 
Ps. you almost always get free desser after a dinner :)

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Engage in the events at the beginning. Even if you don't really like the event in it self, it's a great way to meet other students, and as many students find their main friend groups in the first weeks, it's a great idea to attend in the beginning.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: All systems work poorly and you need to print almost everything

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The open and warm people, the no-stress culture, eating for hours at the tavernas,

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Make an effort to find a nice apartment with a fair landlord/landlady, and likeminded roommates.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Though it's annoying that the university system is inefficient and slow, it means that you don't need to stress either

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Going on beautiful trips with nice people, especially spending the weekends on the beaches of Halkidiki, visiting islands and the bordering countries. Also the good weather (especially April - June) was amazing to live in

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Registration / receiving Academic ID card, living with roommates for the first time, and being surrounded by younger, more energetic, party people for such a long time. Most students were at the age of 20-24 where I was 27/28 and one of the absolute oldest.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
